A_target.statement:
Let $\family {X_i}_{i \mathop \in I}$ be [[Definition:Compact Space|compact]] [[Definition:Topological Space|topological spaces]].
Then $\displaystyle \prod_{i \mathop \in I} X_i$ is compact in the [[Definition:Product Topology|product topology]].

B_source.statement:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be [[Definition:Compact Space|compact spaces]].
Then $X \times Y$ is compact.

substitutions.the finite index set: an arbitrary index set, possibly uncountable
substitutions.the tube lemma argument: an argument on families of closed sets with the finite intersection property

derived.the finite intersection property criteri: compactness restated so that no induction on the index set is needed
derived.the maximal family of closed sets: a family extended by Zorn's lemma, from which a point is read coordinatewise

object_map.reformulation: Restate compactness in a form referring only to finite subfamilies, so no induction on the index set is needed.

validity_conditions: The finite case is proved by induction on the number of factors, which is unavailable for infinite index sets, so the proof must be restructured rather than extended.
Restating compactness by the finite intersection property removes the induction, since the condition refers only to finite subfamilies regardless of the index set.
The general case requires the axiom of choice and is in fact equivalent to it, whereas the finite case does not.
proof_plan: By [[Compact Space satisfies Finite Intersection Axiom]], it suffices to show every family of closed sets with the [[Definition:Finite Intersection Property|finite intersection property]] has non-empty intersection.

Let $\FF$ be a family of subsets of the product with the finite intersection property.
By [[Zorn's Lemma]], extend $\FF$ to a maximal such family $\mathcal M$.

For each $i$, the projections $\set {\map {\pr_i} M: M \in \mathcal M}$ have the finite intersection property in $X_i$.
By compactness of $X_i$, choose $x_i \in \displaystyle \bigcap_{M \mathop \in \mathcal M} \overline {\map {\pr_i} M}$.

Let $x = \family {x_i}$.
Every basic open neighbourhood of $x$ meets every $M \in \mathcal M$, so by maximality belongs to $\mathcal M$.
Hence $x \in \overline M$ for all $M \in \mathcal M$, and $x$ lies in every closed member of $\FF$.
This is [[Tychonoff's Theorem]].
{{qed}}
